newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia FinMin says recession was "foreseeable".
newsitem.headline: Colombia FinMin says recession was "foreseeable".

text.p: In a show of 20/20 economic hindsight, Colombian Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said Monday that the first quarter contraction in gross domestic product was "foreseeable".

The comments contrast sharply with those he made just two days before figures were released in late May, when he denied that the economy had slipped and said it was "impossible to precisely calculate" first quarter GDP.

In the interview with the respected political weekly Semana, Ocampo predicted the economy would return to positive ground before the end of the year. Nonetheless, he said GDP growth would be "below, but not far off" the year's target of between 4 percent and 4.5 percent.
"To a certain point (the first quarter economic results) were foreseeable. Because of advance indicators we knew that February and March figures had been bad," Ocampo said.
Colombia's GDP fell 1.22 percent in the first quarter, following a drop of 0.1 percent in the last quarter of 1996 -- marking the first time in decades that the country has slipped into recession.
Few economic analysts expected such a dramatic slowdown, but were nevertheless surprised by Ocampo's denial of a drop in GDP just two days before the official figures were released.

In the Semana interview, Ocampo said the recession had been sparked by a slowdown in demand. Last week, the influential National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF) argued it was a supply-led recession, driven by poor prospects for returns on investment.

The Finance Minister blamed much of the recession on restrictive monetary policy and said he would like to see interest rates drop another 1.5 percent, effectively bringing them close to the 1997 inflation target of 18 percent.
He also said the slowdown in public spending had depressed the economy.

Ocampo recognized, however, the risk of boosting public spending and further fueling the yawning central government deficit, which ran at around 4 percent of GDP last year and is seen at about 4.2 percent of GDP this year.

"I believe that fiscal adjustment tends to reduce demand. But I also believe we need fiscal adjustment and because of that we have to look for other motors of growth that can substitute public spending," he said.
